title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: Two students discuss a public lecture on black holes and the nature of scientific evidence.

script.en: Did you make it to the astrophysics talk last night? I heard the speaker was quite good.
I did, and it was actually more interesting than I expected. The topic was how black holes form, and she spent a lot of time on this idea of stars that collapse without exploding.
Wait, stars can just disappear without a supernova? I thought every massive star went out with a bang.
That's what I assumed too, but apparently the theory has been around for decades. The problem is that no one has ever directly confirmed a single case.
So how do they study something they can't observe directly?
That's the clever part. They use gravitational wave data from detectors like LIGO. When black holes merge, the waves carry information about their masses and spins.
And that tells them how the black holes were born?

Not exactly, but it gives them clues. She said there's a striking cluster of black holes around ten solar masses, and a strange shortage between twelve and sixteen. That pattern fits the failed-supernova theory.
But she can't prove it, right? It sounds like circumstantial evidence.
She was very honest about that. She said the findings don't confirm the theory, but they match the predictions so closely that it's hard to ignore.
I like that attitude. Some speakers oversell their results.
Exactly. She kept emphasizing that this is a connection between observation and theory, not a final answer. Honestly, it made me want to look into the research myself.
Maybe we should form a study group. I'm taking the astronomy elective next term, and I could use some help with the physics.
I'd be up for that. Let's grab coffee tomorrow and figure out a schedule.

script.en: For decades, astronomers have used light to study the universe, and now a new era of astronomy is listening instead. Gravitational waves are tiny ripples in spacetime, and they were first detected in 2015. These waves now give a powerful way to study objects that give off no light, such as black holes. A recent study led by Caltech researchers used this new tool. It looked into a long-standing mystery: how black holes are born, and most massive stars die in bright supernova explosions. Yet theory suggests some may collapse straight into black holes without any explosion. They would vanish quietly, and the team examined black hole masses from 257 mergers. These were recorded by the LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA detector network. They found that black holes about ten times the Sun's mass were very common. They appeared in about three-quarters of the sample. More surprisingly, there was a clear shortage of black holes between twelve and sixteen solar masses. The researchers also studied how fast the black holes spin. Spin rates can keep clues about the conditions in which they formed. Black holes near ten solar masses tended to have spins in a narrower range than the wider population. Taken together, three things point to a distinct group with a shared history. These are the unusual mass concentration, the scarcity in the twelve-to-sixteen range, and the similar spins. One possible explanation is that many formed from stars that collapsed without exploding. The findings do not confirm the failed-supernova theory, and no such event has ever been directly observed. But the match between data and prediction is striking. It shows how gravitational wave astronomy is starting to link observations with the astrophysics behind them.

sections.title: A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses
sections.passage:
The most massive stars in the universe usually end their lives in spectacular explosions known as supernovae, blasting huge quantities of material into space. Their leftover cores then collapse under gravity, producing neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. Yet scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Rather than exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

New research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. In 2015, LIGO made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions. A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun, and the data suggest that this group may share a common origin.

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample. Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

The researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population. The spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed, so the similarities in rotation offer an additional line of evidence.

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions. The findings do not confirm the theory, but they closely match predictions, showing how gravitational wave astronomy connects observation with underlying astrophysics.
